messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 52
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Judge
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 43

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Anniversaries: The anniversary of the event, Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event, Visual (Uniforms): Military or police uniforms
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark)., Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
  Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At 52, Claire Whitman had spent years cultivating the composed bearing expected of a judge: measured speech, a still face on the bench, a way of listening that revealed little. Before law school and long before her divorce, she had taken a leave from graduate study to work with a humanitarian relief organization in a war zone, a period she once described to colleagues only as “time overseas.” What happened there has remained sharply present to her in ways that do not feel like the past. She recalls one distribution day near the anniversary that now marks her calendar each year without her wanting it to. Armed men in uniform had been moving through the area while civilians crowded around aid supplies. The scene had the heat, dust, and urgency of too many bodies trying to get food and medicine at once. In the middle of that confusion there was shouting, the crack and percussion of gunfire, people dropping and surging, and the metallic chaos of military vehicles and commands barked nearby. She remembers swallowing something handed to her in haste—an oral rehydration solution or ration with a distinct artificial taste—while trying to keep working and realizing, all at once, that terror had overtaken the crowd.

When Claire speaks of it now, she does not recount it as a story with distance. She says that when the memory comes back, she hears the sounds first: the shouted orders, the shots, the crying, as if they are occurring in the room with her. At other times the whole scene arrives at once and feels completely real across all her senses, so that for a moment she is no longer in her chambers or apartment but back there, tasting that same sharp, chemical sweetness in her mouth and feeling the same terror she felt at the time. What unsettles her most is not simply remembering but the total conviction of the reliving. She knows intellectually where she is, yet her body and mind respond as though the event is happening again.

Over the years, certain moments have acquired a particular force. The anniversary of the event approaches each year with a sense of dread she cannot easily explain to anyone around her. She becomes more watchful and more brittle in the weeks before it, sleeping lightly and tracking the date even when she tries not to. Uniforms are difficult in a way that complicates her professional life. Bailiffs, courthouse security officers, and police witnesses are routine features of her work, but she notices their uniforms immediately, often before she has registered anything else about them. She will fix her eyes on paperwork, call a brief recess, or keep conversation clipped and procedural until she feels she has herself back under control. She has also become wary of certain tastes. On more than one occasion, a sports drink or hospital-like electrolyte flavor has abruptly transported her, and she has thrown it away after a single sip, disturbed by how fast the courtroom and the present can disappear.

Claire has tried to manage all this by narrowing her life. She avoids circumstances that remind her of the war zone, including darkness; if she is invited to evening events, she often declines or leaves before dusk, telling people she has an early start. She keeps lamps on in her apartment and television murmuring in the background rather than sit in a dark room. She works hard to control her emotions and regards any sign of visible feeling as dangerous exposure. In court this looks like exceptional discipline; privately it means she clamps down on tears, anger, and fear with equal force. She tries just as hard not to think about the trauma at all. If an image intrudes, she turns immediately to briefs, opinions, or administrative tasks, anything to push it away.

The cost has been a growing sense of separateness. Claire has come to believe that other people can see what happened to her just by looking at her, as though the experience is stamped on her face despite all her efforts at composure. She sits apart at judicial conferences, declines collegial dinners, and keeps even friends at a formal distance. Since her divorce she has lived alone, and although she does not describe herself as lonely so much as cut off, she feels set apart from others in a way she cannot bridge. Underneath that distance is a broader conviction that the world is dangerous. She says this matter-of-factly, not as philosophy but as fact learned once and never unlearned.

She sought help only recently, after the anniversary coincided with a week of criminal hearings requiring repeated contact with uniformed officers. During one session, the taste of an electrolyte drink left on the bench by a clerk hit her unexpectedly, and for a few seconds she heard the old sounds so vividly that she gripped the armrest and lost track of the testimony in front of her. No one in the courtroom seemed to notice, yet afterward she was shaken by the sense that she could no longer guarantee her control. Coming to treatment felt humiliating and necessary in equal measure. What she fears most is that the world she has always believed to be dangerous will break into the present without warning and expose her in public. What she hopes for, cautiously, is not to erase what happened but to live in a way that is no longer organized around bracing for its return.
